newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's May note default ratio falls from April.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's May note default ratio falls from April.

text.p: The ratio of South Korea's defaults on notes in May fell to 0.23 percent from 0.25 percent in April, but was still higher than 0.12 percent recorded in May 1996, the central Bank of Korea said on Sunday.
The ratio in April was the highest level in 15 months.
The notes include promissory notes and bank cheques.
The bank said in a report the ratio eased in May despite a series of defaults on debt payments by Samlip General Foods Co and its affiliates during the month.
Samlip, the nation's leading confectioner, has filed for court receivership after defaulting on debt payments.
The bank attributed the lower default ratio to the fading impact of two large failures earlier this year.
The nation's second-largest steelmaker Hanbo Steel Co collapsed in January and specialty stainless steel products maker Sammi Steel Co collapsed in March.
The report said 1.70 trillion won worth of notes were not honoured in May out of a total 734.5 trillion won called in.
The number of defaulting companies increased to 1,257 in May from 935 a year ago. But it was slightly less than 1,318 firms that failed to honour notes in April.
